prompt: What does `git log` record about a change to `prompts/triage.txt`, and what does it leave out?

choices.text: The score before and after, but not the diff
choices.why: Git knows nothing about scores.

choices.text: Everything, if the messages are long enough
choices.why: Even long messages are read only by somebody running `git log`.

choices.text: What and when, and almost never why it was made
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Why it was made, but not when
choices.why: The date is always there; the reason rarely is.

prompt: A new teammate finds the JSON examples hard to read and wants to rewrite them as plain lines. Why will the history probably not stop them?

choices.text: Nobody reads a log for reasons, and it has none
choices.why: Right: the revert says what, not why.

choices.text: The plain-lines commit was deleted from the history
choices.why: It is there, as `86913c0`.

choices.text: Git does not keep commits older than a month
choices.why: It keeps every commit.

choices.text: Plain lines are forbidden by the JSON instruction
choices.why: The instruction says nothing about the examples.

prompt: Match each note to the question it answers.

pairs.right: What has gone wrong before, and what stops it again?
What is this, how good is it, and what does it cost?

prompt: Why does the lesson keep these notes beside the prompt rather than in long commit messages?

choices.text: Commit messages cannot hold more than one line
choices.why: They can hold any number.

choices.text: Git does not allow tables in commit messages
choices.why: It stores any text.

choices.text: Notes beside the prompt are hashed into its id
choices.why: Only the prompt file is hashed.

choices.text: Whoever opens the prompt reads notes beside it
choices.why: Right: commit messages are read by somebody already in `git log`.

prompt: Where does the form of a decision record come from, as the lesson tells it?

choices.text: Cohen's 1960 paper on agreement
choices.why: That is kappa.

choices.text: Michael Nygard's post on architecture decisions
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Google's book on site reliability engineering
choices.why: That is the failure log's precedent.

choices.text: The paper on model cards by Mitchell and others
choices.why: That is the prompt card's.

prompt: Why does the record list the options that lost, with their numbers?

choices.text: The sign test needs at least three options
choices.why: A sign test compares two runs.

choices.text: Options that lost must be deleted from the prompt file
choices.why: They were never in the file together.

choices.text: The rejected option is the one the next person proposes
choices.why: Right: and here it is the one somebody already tried.

choices.text: Git needs them to compute the diff
choices.why: Git knows nothing about the record's content.

prompt: The part of a decision record that names the conditions under which the decision would become wrong is headed `Revisit ___`.
Dev favoured plain examples by three and the holdout favoured JSON by three, both with large p. What does record 0001 do with that?

choices.text: Says the sets cannot separate them, and why
choices.why: Right: a judgement, named as one.

choices.text: Reports only the dev result, since dev came first
choices.why: That is the record that makes the next person repeat the run.

choices.text: Picks plain lines, since 27 is more than 24
choices.why: Three messages with p = 0.375 is not a finding.

choices.text: Refuses to decide until the p falls below 0.05
choices.why: A prompt has to be one or the other meanwhile.

prompt: Which of these changes deserves a decision record rather than a sentence in its commit message?
hint: A real choice that somebody would reverse.

choices.text: Renaming a run file
choices.why: Run files are not the prompt.

choices.text: Escaping the message with `|xml`
choices.why: No reasonable person would undo it; a sentence is enough.

choices.text: Fixing a typo in the field list
choices.why: Nothing was weighed.

choices.text: The shape of the examples
choices.why: Right: somebody changed it and somebody changed it back.

prompt: According to the lesson, what is a failure log entry about?

choices.text: Only failures that have been fixed
choices.why: An open failure belongs in the log too.

choices.text: The system, and not who made the edit
choices.why: Right: blameless.

choices.text: The person whose change caused it
choices.why: That is what the practice exists to avoid.

choices.text: The model's provider and its terms
choices.why: The entry is about the prompt and its checks.

prompt: How many of the forty dev replies under `prompts/triage.txt` were cut at an apostrophe and failed `json`?
A customer message is answered wrongly in production, and the prompt is fixed. What finishes the fix, according to the lesson?

choices.text: A note in the commit message
choices.why: A note cannot fail a change.

choices.text: Raising the temperature to avoid the same reply
choices.why: That adds variation, not a guard.

choices.text: The message, cleaned, as a case in a test set
choices.why: Right: otherwise the gate has nothing to fail on.

choices.text: A reply to the customer apologising for the error
choices.why: That is support, not the fix.

prompt: In an entry, the line `Caught by` reads *nothing would have*. Why does the lesson call that the most important line?

choices.text: It is a hole in the tests
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It means the failure cannot happen again
choices.why: It means nothing would see it happen again.

choices.text: It means the entry can be deleted
choices.why: It is the entry most worth keeping.

choices.text: It shows the person who made the edit
choices.why: The entry is blameless.

prompt: Which published idea does the prompt card follow?

choices.text: Architecture decision records, by Nygard
choices.why: That is the decision record.

choices.text: Blameless postmortems, from Google's book
choices.why: That is the failure log.

choices.text: MT-Bench, by Zheng and others
choices.why: That is about judges.

choices.text: Model cards
choices.why: Right.

prompt: The card shows dev 24/40 and attacks 3/10. Why does the lesson call the attacks score the most important line?

choices.text: Dev scores are not allowed on a card
choices.why: Dev is on the card too.

choices.text: It shows what must guard the labels
choices.why: Right: a person, or least privilege.

choices.text: It is the highest of the four scores
choices.why: It is the lowest share.

choices.text: Attacks are the only set a person labelled
choices.why: Every set was labelled by a person.

prompt: `stats.py` reports 12246 input tokens over the forty dev calls. How many input tokens per call is that? One decimal place.
Why should the card carry the prompt id and the commit?
hint: What do the numbers belong to?

choices.text: Because the id is the owner's name, encoded
choices.why: It is a hash of the file.

choices.text: Because Ollama reads the card before each call
choices.why: Ollama never sees it.

choices.text: So its numbers point at their exact version
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: So the card can be found by `git log`
choices.why: The card is found beside the prompt.

prompt: Which of these belong on the card, as the lesson writes it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: What it is not for
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Every test set's score
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The known failures
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Only the best score of the four
choices.why: Printing only the best would mislead everybody.
